On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I regret very much the necessity of once more calling attention to the fact that a certain return I asked for away back in February has not yet been tabled, unless it was done to-day. Possibly, if it has been tabled to-day, the Secretary of State will so inform me and I shall require to say no more.
What is the return?

I wish to direct the attention of the house to the fact that apart from some comparatively unimportant communications which were apparently obtained by the Department of External Affairs, the order that was passed by this house has not been complied with, nor has there been any valid or indeed any kind of excuse for noncompliance with this order. I wish to read the order and I shall endeavour not to depart from the strict letter of my duty in speaking to a question of privilege. The order reads:
Return to an order of the House of Commons, dated 12th February, 1934, showing:
A copy of all correspondence, cables and other documents, exchanged between the Hon. Herbert Marler, Canadian representative in Tokyo, Japan, or the representative of any other country, and any member of the federal government, with respect to the possibility and practicability of disposing of more Canadian farm products, especially wheat and wheat flour, either in Japan or China, during the past three and a half years.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that in this day of stirring events this is a comparatively unimportant return; but that depends, I may say, on what it may contain. I think there is prospect of something very important being in it if I can only get the Minister of Trade and1 Commerce (Mr. Stevens), in whose possession it is, to table it. I have waited long and patiently, as I think you will agree, for this return. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether we can get a little order; I cannot hear myself talking. I know that we will-have to forgive them under the circumstances and events of yesterday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The days that it
should have taken to comply with the order have extended into weeks and the weeks into months-four months and nine or ten days;' yet the order has not made its appearance. Since the events of yesterday have passed, it occurred to me that this would be the

psychological time, when the government is in particularly good humour, to come across with this return. I have done nearly everything an hon. member can do. I cannot go across the aisle and commit some act of violence, especially when I know the report is not there or it would have been tabled to-day; and it might not be a safe performance to indulge in anyway. Seriously, I feel that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, according to his own officers, has a report from the Hon. Mr. Marler on the question of selling more wheat to China or Japan, and he simply has not tabled it. He has flouted the command of the house; he has refused to obey, without giving any kind of excuse I have heard yet. I will now give the minister an opportunity of either saying that he will table it or giving a valid reason why he cannot or won't.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not quite fair in his attitude to-day, and on reflection I think he will recognize that he is not. As a matter of fact, everything which it is proper to file has been filed. Certain documents may pass between one department and another or between the minister representing this government in Japan, as in this case, and the Department of External Affairs, which it is not proper or competent for the government to bring down. Such documents as we could bring down we have brought down I went further, in my desire to assist the hon. member, and asked1 my officers to go over matters with me so that we might try to bring before him anything which it was within our power to bring down. Furthermore, I asked the head of the commercial intelligence branch to look over the files to see whether he could find any interesting or helpful information or documents there, and these are now in process of being prepared, as I am informed by my officers, and will be forwarded to the hon. member. But he had not asked for such documents; that is done purely as an act of courtesy to him. So far as the technical obligations of the government are concerned, they have been fully complied with.

I do not think I
can speak a second time on a question of privilege, can I? All I say is that four months of courtesy is delightful, but four minutes of action would be better.

The house resumed from Friday, June 15, consideration in committee of Bill No. 99, to amend the Income War Tax Act-Mr. Rhodes -Mr. Sullivan in the chair.
On section 14-Non-residents deemed to be carrying on business.

While the bill is before committee I presume the Prime Minister is in charge of it. I want to point out that the other day clause 8 was passed along with a number of other clauses without any discussion. I wonder whether the Prime Minister could give the committee an explanation if he would permit me to refer to clause 8, subclause 6.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let us first dispose of the clause before the committee. This clause stood at the instance of the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury).
Carried.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Had it not stood, the necessity of preparing a large amount of in-

Income War Tax Act
formation which I thought the hon. member wanted with respect to it would have been obviated. I am very glad to dispense with the reading of the information.
I have in the meantime received some of the information and I am quite satisfied.
Section agreed to.

Would the Prime Minister kindly allow me to refer to clause 8, subclause 6, and to direct his attention to the particular point I have in mind? This subelause seems to be a provision against non-residents. It has been, I understand, a principle in income tax legislation that non-residents shall not be taxed in view of the fact that our residents do not expect to be taxed in a foreign country. After all, the matter works out pretty fairly. If you tax a non-resident he receives exemption from his tax in his own country, and if a foreign country taxes our residents they get an exemption here, so by and large, the matter works out evenly. But I submit to my right hon. friend that this particular clause invades an entirely new field of taxation, and with all due deference I think there is considerable objection to it. Perhaps the Prime Minister would indicate whether there is some particular case-and by that I mean not a particular individual case but class of cases-which has been dealt with, which justifies a departure from the general rule.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman is aware quite as well as I am, that there has been a tendency on the part of all countries during recent years to make more drastic provisions in their income tax laws. In Great Britain, the United States and other countries it has been the practice in recent years to secure so far as possible a tax from any corporation or individual making an income in the particular country. It will be remembered that in the United States for a time they required a certificate that all taxes had been paid before a person was allowed to board a ship at New York to go abroad, and similar provisions have been made with respect to receipts for money received by artists and even by prizefighters in cities of the United States. In this country we have been endeavouring slowly to develop our income tax law. For instance, clause 14 that stood goes back as a matter of fact to 1924, it being put upon the statute books then.
Has that clause ever been operative?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, perhaps $56,000 were secured under it last year.
With respect to clause 8, subclause 6, although it has been passed, I am making this: explanation which is given without my attention being directed to it with care. It will' be observed that subclause 6 reads:
The income for any taxation period of a non-resident beneficiary of any estate or trust shall be deemed to include all income accruing: to the credit of the non-resident beneficiary, whether received by him or not during such taxation period, and such non-resident beneficiary shall be liable to taxation in respect of such incomes as in the ease of an unmarried person resident in Canada: provided that he shall not be entitled to the exemptions provided by paragraphs (e) and (i) of subsection one of section five of this act. The tax payable hereunder shall be deducted by the trustee from any amount otherwise payable to such beneficiary and remitted to the receiver general of Canada.
The family corporation we have wiped out. The personal corporation still exists; that is, if John Smith desires to incorporate his estate and call it John Smith, Limited, he may do so. He may not disburse all the revenues coming from that estate in any particular year; what he may do is retain the income during the year and reinvest it, but under the law as it now stands he is liable for tax. There was some difficulty about this point but it has been cleared up and the practice now is to tax the income regardless as to whether it has been disbursed. The income tax branch advises the Department of Finance that in this country there are large numbers of trusts created by non-residents, and these trusts have been, shall I say, profitable inasmuch as they have substantial incomes which in some instances are not disbursed and are reinvested for those who own the fund, that is, those who created the trust. This proposes that the income thus derived from the operations of a trust in Canada shall pay tax in the same way as a personal corporation would do. I am not unaware of the fact that this matter has been discussed on previous occasions-and I am now speaking, as I say, without having carefully gone into it-and the suggestion has been made that the effect of taxing the income of such trusts would be to militate against money coming into this country for investment, But any tax thus paid by a beneficiary under the trust would in most cases be free from taxation at least in the country in which the creator, or the settler, if you will, resides. Either in Great Britain or the United States that would be a taxable deduction from his income for the current year; that is, assuming that the income of the trust in this country was sufficient to create a tax of $500, he would be entitled in Great Britain or the United
Income War Tax Act

States, on production of evidence that tha-t tax was paid here, to set that up as a deduction against his income tax. In Great Britain they tax such trust incomes in the manner I have just indicated. I know the income tax branch have given a great deal of attention to this matter and they have concluded there is no reason why a trust set up by non-residents and producing substantial income should be treated differently from a personal corporation established in this country by one of our own citizens in his lifetime. The enforcement of this provision with respect to trusts has been limited to those originated, shall I say, by persons who resided in countries where a deduction is allowed from the income tax payable by them of the amount paid on the income from the trust here. I think that is as clear a statement as I can make from my understanding of the provision.

I did not catch the numbers the Prime Minister gave last night as to the bills that were coming up for discussion to-day, and although I made inquiries I did not know this one was coming up. I wonder whether the Prime Minister would allow the bill to stand in committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, I had intended to move the bill forward to-day. Frankly, I do not think the government is prepared to abandon the provision.
I am not talking about abandoning it. I want to mention just one matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This clause has been passed.
In committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The bill stood for one purpose only, that is in regard to clause 14, and the hon. gentleman who asked that that clause stand now says that he is satisfied about it because it was put into the statutes of 1924. But I always like to accommodate hon. gentlemen opposite. The bill has to go to the Senate, but if he desires it to stand I will not press it to-day.

I telephoned this afternoon to the commissioner of taxation and I found he was at the house. The point I have in mind is, the Prime Minister's explanation indicated that the bill is directed towards the income of Canadian trusts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of trusts established in Canada.

I point out that the bill does not seem to provide for that. I wanted to look at the bill and see if that amendment should not be made, if the government has decided upon the policy of taxing nonresidents, as to the advisability of which I have some doubts. I think the bill should, as the Prime Minister's explanation indicates, be confined to estates or trusts established in Canada. Perhaps the Prime Minister would allow it to stand for an hour or two-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But I desire to point out that our taxing arm does not reach to other than Canadian trusts.

I think the Prime Minister forgets that we have lengthened our taxing arm by directing that taxes shall be deducted at the source. Therefore you may have a trust established in Great Britain or France or somewhere with regard to Canadian securities, and your taxing arm will reach there because you deduct the tax where the bond interest or the dividend is paid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But not the source in the sense in which the hon. gentleman used the word a moment ago. Our taxing arm cannot compel any corporation in Great Britain or France to do anything. What we can tax is the income here from the Canadian investment. But our taxing arm does not touch the corporation in Great Britain or France, but only the income in this country.
I desire further to point out that subsection 6 does not tax non-residents. Let us get that out of our head. AVhat we are taxing is the income in this country that may belong to people not in this country. That is an altogether different thing. What we are taxing is income, not individuals.
I do not see that distinction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well I think most people will agree that there is a very clear distinction between saying that you are taxing an income accruing outside of the country and taxing an income in this country that belongs to a person not residing in it. Surely if the money is earned in this country it is not unfair to do what they do in Great Britain and France, namely tax it here, although the person in receipt of it may be in China or India. In the United States very large sums are being collected on just such trusts set up there. I suppose it is known to the hon. gentleman from his reading that very large sums of money have been invested in the United States in that form by those who reside in many countries of Europe. In that

Canadian-British Insurance
country they have stretched out their arm not against the individual but against the money. It is not a non-resident tax, it is a tax against money made under the protection of the institutions of the country. The contribution that is made by those who have thus obtained the income comes out of the money so secured. I know the argument against it, that it discourages the coming in of funds from abroad; that the trusts will no longer continue. That has always been the argument. I find that in other countries where that argument has been disregarded there has been no such result. People continue to invest where they think it safe and where they can secure under reasonably sound conditions the largest income. Out of that income we take something because the protection of our laws and the institutions of our country have enabled the profit to be obtained.
However I move that the committee rise and ask leave to sit again this day in order to meet the hon. gentleman's view, although as a matter of fact I have not moved that we reconsider the section. But we can carry on the discussion without doing that.
Progress reported.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 72, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932.
He said: It is proposed to amend this legislation in very important particulars. The bill has passed the Senate and comes to us from that chamber. As it stands it is intended to secure to life insurance companies carrying on business in Canada the right to obtain a licence from the insurance department of this country. Companies other than life insurance companies of course are also involved. I need hardly point out to this house what is very well known, that the last judgment of the privy council made it clear beyond peradventure that the business of insurance is within the exclusive jurisdiction *of the provinces. Nevertheless there are certain features of insurance business, life insurance business in particular, that require to be considered from the standpoint of insolvency, from the standpoint of interest and other standpoints that fall solely within the jurisdiction of this parliament. Eminent counsel have been engaged from time to time by those who are greatly concerned, because I need hardly point out to this house how anxious companies carrying on life insurance
business are to have a licence from the Dominion of Canada, especially when carrying on business in foreign jurisdictions; they have found it valuable to have the actuarial experience of this dominion under the direction of the superintendent of insurance-
If hon. gentlemen in the rear will be good enough to go into the lobbies to talk there rather than here, I suggest it would be better.
The effect of securing the licence, of course, is to indicate that the actuarial department under the direction of the superintendent of insurance have satisfied themselves of the solvency of the company securing the licence The benefits that have accrued to Canadian companies doing business abroad by having that licence have been very great. I think I indicated in this house on one occasion that a Canadian company has at risk in the United States of America over a billion dollars of insurance in all forms, and many millions are at risk in other countries, as well as in Canada. So this bill was prepared on the assumption that this comes within the legislative competence of parliament.
There are certain sections to which attention was specifically directed the other day, that is it is proposed to withdraw certain insurance companies or organizations or associations from the operation of the bill.
Lloyds?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. So^ that the principle of the bill may be explained in a single sentence, as being that jurisdiction should be established for the parliament of Canada, if possible, in the manner indicated, for companies that desire to secure licences under our act to enable them to have the benefit of such expression of approval in the carrying on of their business in other countries.

I want
to congratulate the government on withdrawing from this bill the clause affecting Lloyds. I may say that I read with great interest the debate that occurred on this subject in another place and I was not impressed by the learned legal argument of the leader of the Senate in regard to the question of bankruptcy and insolvency as affecting Lloyds. His argument was that the privy council would be influenced on this question because the suggestion of bankruptcy or insolvency could not be thought of in connection with such a wonderful company as Lloyds. Those who are interested in the history of Lloyds and who desire to be fully informed may consult the articles in the Encyclopaedia Britannica, where they will find a very full history of its operations. The magnitude of its operations now is almost beyond our comprehension. In every part of the world they transact business. They have had risks in Canada for many, many years, and they have very large risks in this country at the present time, and in fact are authorized in the province of Quebec to carry on business. Provisions have been specifically made, and if the committee so desire I might indicate what they are, with respect to this company carrying on business in various parts of Canada. The organization of the company is such that they are not in a position to withdraw from their funds the deposit that is required by our law without amending their own legislation, and they have indicated that as they have grown up more or less under the aegis of the board of trade in England they do not desire to take that course. During the war their risks were enormous and in every part of the world.
I make this statement in order that there might be no misapprehension or doubt on the part of anyone in this parliament or in Canada as to the solvency of the company or as to its ability to discharge its obligations. Lloyds register indeed is the last word to which those who seek information in respect to maritime matters refer. Their captains' room in London is resorted to by men from every part of the world, and their means of information with respect to the whereabouts of every ship on the registers of the various countries of the world is really most remarkable. If any hon. members of this house happen to look up the shipping columns of the morning papers in London and notice the whereabouts of different ships in all parts of the world, they will find that if there is a casualty even to a very small ship it is always recorded there. I was not here when the supplementary estimates were passed the other day. There was an item in connection with the disarmament conference, and I should like to know from the Prime Minister whether Canada has representation at the present time at the conference or on the committees which sit in connection with the disarmament conference; also who this representative is or these representatives are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
probably aware of the fact that since the formal adjournment of the committee on disarmament no action has been taken other than the endeavour by the great powers, if I might use that word in the broad sense, to secure some form of agreement with respect to disarmament. The hon. gentleman, who follows these matters with great care, will remember the proposals put forward by various countries and finally the effort made by the British government to secure some form of acquiescence on the part of all-or agreement, which is the word I should use-and that the Lord Privy Seal visited various capitals looking towards that end. The result has not been
very satisfactory. The speech made a few days ago by the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom indicated the great differences of opinion that prevail among the great powers with respect to this matter. The effort that is now being made to secure, through membership in the League of Nations of all the powers, the opportunity to enable one body to deal with the subject is still going forward. The hon. gentleman is perhaps more familiar with what has been done in that regard than I am. Our position is being constantly watched, and that position is communicated to us by dispatches which come in from the foreign office. We are kept advised of what is going on from that source, and our permanent representative at Geneva, Doctor Riddell, is constantly informed as to what is transpiring there; and when occasion necessitates we have representation from the Paris office of the dominion to proceed to Geneva for the purpose of discussion. But until matters reach what I might very properly describe as a somewhat nearer approach to unity on the great principles that have to be considered, I should think it is not at all probable that we shall endeavour to make representations other than in the manner I have indicated. We are willing to make, and are de-sirious of making, any contribution we can; but the contribution that we can make, in the very nature of things, is very limited until the moment comes when by agreement between the great powers we are able at least to throw the weight of our vote and influence towards the acceptance of a plan of disarmament that will bring about the result aimed at. And that, as I say, is not at the moment as promising as one would like. I do not think I can usefully say more than that.
What has Canada got to disarm? We have nothing to disarm in this country. The fact that we talk about disarmament implies armament.
It should not be necessary for us to go to Europe for the purpose of bringing about disarmament, but we want to cooperate and try to get other nations to disarm.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) will agree that while a country may not find itself so situated as to have to disarm, because it is in the happy position of having nothing to disarm, its moral influence and the weight of its example, especially having regard to its geographical position, is a matter of great importance. While it is true that we are but

ten and a half millions, and while it is true that we have no armament to destroy or to scrap, nevertheless we have, as a member of the league, a voice and a vote; and to the extent that they may be available for the purpose of promoting the cause of peace, I regard them as being of importance at this particular time. It is not necessary of course, as the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) says, to send a delegation or to maintain them in Europe for that purpose; but at any moment when voice and vote become important we have the facilities through our Paris office of exercising such influence as can be brought to bear by both our vote and our voice.

Do I understand then
that the amount which is being voted in connection with the disarmament conference is to be used in case the government finds it necessary to send somebody in addition to Doctor Riddell to take part in the proceedings?

speechtext:

quite right in that assumption. If, for instance, a situation should develop in which those charged with larger responsibilities than we have think it desirable that there should be a general meeting, and we should have to send someone from this country, the vote is to be available for that purpose; and in addition to that it is only fair to say that we cannot charge against the Paris office the expense of going to Geneva out of their meagre surplus, and a proper charge against that $5,000 would be expenses incurred for that purpose.

I did not know whether I would have another opportunity to ask the question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.

Am I in order in asking the Prime Minister this question:	When an
order is given to a manufacturer of cloth, would it be possible to induce him to use more Canadian wool in orders for cloth when contracts are awarded by the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kamouraska may be amazed to know a few days ago I was discussing with representatives of the woollen industry the possibility of the utilization of our wool, and I was surprised to learn the extent to which it has been and is being used at the present time in local mills throughout the country. But it would be very difficult in contracts to do more than suggest that the wool be of Canadian manufacture. I do not know how we could very well go beyond that, because the cloth that
is standardized for some requirements of the public service is standardized on the basis of there being utilized with Canadian wool, wool that is imported sometimes from Australia, sometimes from Australia by way of England and sometimes from New Zealand, as the hon. gentleman knows.

Schedule agreed to.
Schedule B and C agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Since the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) mentioned the matter he did this afternoon with respect to clause 8 of Bill 99, a slip has been placed in my hands stating that a delegation is arriving here to-morrow morning and desires to make representations with reference to the Income War Tax Act. I will therefore let the matter stand until to-morrow, although the clause has been passed, if that meets with the convenience of the hon. gentleman.
A telegram to the same effect has just been received, so I take it that we can let the matter stand.

I was just telephoning the commissioner and suggesting a possible amendment he might submit to the Prime Minister. I did not know anything about the delegation. I am only too glad if the bill is allowed to stand.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. Ill, to repeal the Finance Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sullivan in the chair.
On section 1-Finance Act repealed.

I would just like to suggest to the Prime Minister that although we have [DOT] not had very much time to consider this bill, perhaps it might be a good idea to leave the Finance Act on the statute book. We are going to set up a privately owned Bank of Canada, which is to have the sole right of note issue. If there should ever be a conflict of opinion between the government and that bank as to whether there were enough currency issued and available in Canada the
Finance Act

government of the day might be very glad to have the Finance Act on the statute book. I do not see what harm it would do. I make that suggestion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman is serious in making that suggestion. If that act were to remain and the Bank of Canada Act were to come into force it would mean absolute chaos. The hon. gentleman always refers to the Bank of Canada as a privately owned bank. That matter, I believe, is to be discussed in the committee later.
That is why they want it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I am just coming to that. The profits that are earned by the Bank of Canada are for the people of Canada, with the exception of four and a half per cent interest on the capital, which it would probably cost even if the money were borrowed. As to maintaining the Finance Act and the Bank of Canada Act in force at the same time, it would create financial chaos; it would be destructive of the whole system as we maintain it, and public confidence would disappear.

Does the Prime Minister anticipate that there will be any hiatus between the coming into force of the Bank of Canada Act and the repeal of the Finance Act? I was going to ask whether the action on each could not be concurrent, one to come into force when the other is repealed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has asked a question which I asked myself when this statute was being prepared. The banks have loans under the Finance Act. Matters will have to be cleaned up, so to speak, and under the act as it now stands it is contemplated that for certain obligations the central bank shall receive certain forms of securities from the dominion.
There will perhaps be some overlapping?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This seems to be the safer method to pursue in view of the possibilities of overlapping in the operation of the act. As a matter of fact the course suggested was that which was originally being pursued, but on looking into the matter I thought this the safer method, to set up the institution so that it may function successfully, and repeal this act whenever the overlapping, if there be any, has been ended; or it may be that it can be arranged to have it done at the same time.

Even if the Finance Act is not repealed, as long as the central bank is carrying on I anticipate no attempt would be made to use the Finance Act. I simply suggest it might be left so that it could be used at any time if the government so desired.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not want to be discourteous to the hon. gentleman, but I think if he will take a few moments to consider he will realize that an application might be made by a chartered bank to the government for advances under that act, and the government no longer having any money with which to make the advance because the engraving and issuing of dominion notes would have ceased, a situation would be created which in my humble judgment would be more or less ridiculous.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

What is the relation of this bill to the one introduced yesterday to amend the Dominion Notes Act?

speechtext:
That is the act under
which in 1915 Dominion of Canada notes or bills were issued on the security of (a) certain railway bonds-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, not $26,000,000, but
$16,000,000 and $10,000,000. The $16,000,000 was on railway securities and the $10,000,000 on the general credit of the country. Obviously this liability must be taken care of when the new bank begins to function under the provisions set forth in the bill incorporating the bank. The act itself provides how that liability shall be discharged. In order that there shall be no difficulty about the matter this bill repeals that act on proclamation when the other act comes into force.

Finance Act

Were
these 826,000.000 included in the total of
8171.000,000 given yesterday?

I recall that last session the Pr ne Minister in making a statement told the house that during the war an issue of something like sixty or sixty-five million dollars of currency was made for which no coverage was supplied. Under what act was that done? I should also like to ask whether the announcement made yesterday with regard to the changed standards will take care of that old inflation, if I might call it so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no. Under the provisions of the War Measures Act certain issues were made. They were retired and disposed of except those covered by this statute, which are of a permanent character. The $16,000,000 is secured now by railway securities; the other $10,000,000 is on the general credit of the country. Both of them are to be taken care of under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act that I referred to yesterday, and the changed coverage provisions that are set forth in the amendment to the statute that appears upon the order paper as Bill No. 110.
That is the $60,000,000 odd?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: But last year I can remember that $60,000,000 was spoken of. That has been reduced to the sum mentioned here, I take it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: That would mean gold was not held?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, under the provision requiring dollar for dollar above the stipulated amount.
And whereas it is expedient that such issues, and the making of such advances and the taking of security therefor, and the agreements with regard to repayment of such advances be severally confirmed:
Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1.	The issues of dominion notes and the advances made in pursuance of the orders in council cited in the preamble, and all things done under the provisions of the said orders in council, are hereby confirmed and shall be deemed to have been duly authorized.
2.	The agreements referred to in the preamble are hereby declared to be and shall be deemed to have been valid agreements and binding on the respective railway companies parties thereto.
That is the authority for the issue of the
S26,000,000, $16,000,000 being covered by the
securities of the railways guaranteed by the dominion, and the 810.000,000 being uncovered.
